    Classical refinement 21

    G000001Zariski topologyTopology

    Classical refinement · Structure · Separated schemes of finite type over a separated Noetherian base S; see individual edge scope.

    Jointly surjective open immersions. On the finite-type site one can take finite families, including the empty cover of the empty scheme.

    Points. For the Gabber–Kelly finite-type site, the affine local test objects are spectra of local rings.

    References
    Stacks 020K · topologies on schemes · Gabber–Kelly, Definition 2.5, Theorem 2.6 and Table 1 · Stacks 020O · Zariski covering

    G000002Nisnevich topologyTopology

    Classical refinement · Structure · Separated schemes of finite type over a separated Noetherian base S; see individual edge scope.

    Completely decomposed étale families: every target point has a lift whose induced residue-field map is an isomorphism.

    Points. For the Gabber–Kelly finite-type site, the affine local test objects are spectra of henselian local rings.

    References
    Gabber–Kelly, Definition 2.5, Theorem 2.6 and Table 1

    G000004Smooth topologyTopology

    Classical refinement · Structure · Separated schemes of finite type over a separated Noetherian base S; see individual edge scope.

    Jointly surjective smooth families. Smooth surjections admit sections étale locally on the target, so their generated topology is already étale.

    Points. For the Gabber–Kelly finite-type site, the affine local test objects are spectra of strictly henselian local rings (by equality with étale).

    References
    Stacks 055U · étale-local sections of smooth morphisms · Stacks 020K · topologies on schemes · Stacks 021Z · smooth covering

    G000006Fppf topologyTopology

    Classical refinement · Structure · Separated schemes of finite type over a separated Noetherian base S; see individual edge scope.

    Jointly surjective flat morphisms locally of finite presentation. Over a locally Noetherian target, finite flat maps are finite locally free; in general use finite locally free maps in the generation theorem.

    G000007Fpqc topologyTopology

    Classical refinement · Structure · Separated schemes of finite type over a separated Noetherian base S; see individual edge scope.

    Flat families for which each affine open of the target is covered by images of finitely many quasi-compact opens in the sources that map into that affine open. In particular a faithfully flat quasi-compact morphism is a singleton cover.

    References
    Stacks 022A · fpqc coverings · Stacks 03NV · the fpqc topology · Stacks 022B · fpqc covering

    G000008Canonical topologyTopology

    Classical refinement · Structure · Separated schemes of finite type over a separated Noetherian base S; see individual edge scope.

    The finest topology for which every representable presheaf is a sheaf. A sieve covers precisely when it is universally effective epimorphic, tested by descent of maps into every object after each base change.

    References
    Stacks 00WO · representable sheaves and the canonical topology · Stacks 03NV · fpqc subcanonicity · Stacks 00ZA · canonical topology · Stacks 00Z9 · finest topology making given presheaves sheaves

    G000009Qfh topologyTopology

    Classical refinement · Structure · Separated schemes of finite type over a separated Noetherian base S; see individual edge scope.

    On the finite-type site one may take finite families of quasi-finite maps whose coproduct is a universal topological epimorphism (a quotient map after all base changes).

    Points. For the Gabber–Kelly finite-type site, the affine local test objects are spectra of absolutely integrally closed local domains.

    References
    Gabber–Kelly, Definition 2.5, Theorem 2.6 and Table 1

    G000012Prime-to-ℓ finite flat topologyTopology

    Classical refinement · Structure · Separated schemes of finite type over a separated Noetherian base S; see individual edge scope.

    Fix a prime ℓ. Use singleton finite flat surjections of constant rank d with ℓ ∤ d. Such maps are finite locally free in the finite-type Noetherian setting.

    References
    Gabber–Kelly, Definition 2.5, Theorem 2.6 and Table 1

    G000020ℓdh topologyTopology

    Classical refinement · Structure · Separated schemes of finite type over a separated Noetherian base S; see individual edge scope.

    Fix a prime ℓ. Adjoin prime-to-ℓ finite flat surjections to cdh covers.

    Points. For the Gabber–Kelly finite-type site, the affine local test objects are spectra of henselian valuation rings whose fraction fields have no nontrivial finite extension of degree prime to ℓ.

    References
    Gabber–Kelly, Definition 2.5, Theorem 2.6 and Table 1

    G000023Ph topologyTopology

    Valuative refinement · Structure · The common qcqs ambient category specified in the valuative diagram.

    Use Zariski covers and proper surjections as generators. The Stacks Project distinguishes ph from its finite-presentation h convention. Over the separated finite-type Noetherian site of the classical comparison these are the same generators used there for h.

    G000024Valuative (v) topologyTopology

    Valuative refinement · Structure · The common qcqs ambient category specified in the valuative diagram.

    For a map of qcqs schemes Y→XY\to X, test every Spec⁡V→X\operatorname{Spec}V\to X for a valuation ring VV. There must be an injective local map of valuation rings V↪WV\hookrightarrow W and a lift Spec⁡W→Y\operatorname{Spec}W\to Y over XX. For families, work affine locally on the target and take finite affine refinements whose disjoint union passes the test.

    References
    Bhatt–Mathew, The arc-topology · Stacks 0ETA · valuation lifting and comparison with fpqc and ph · Stacks 0EVM · affine inverse limits of h and ph covers

    Stacks index 0ETA 0EVM

    G000025Arc topologyTopology

    Valuative refinement · Structure · The common qcqs ambient category specified in the valuative diagram.

    Use the same lifting test but restrict both valuation rings VV and WW to rank at most one. Rank zero includes fields. For families use the corresponding affine-local finite refinement convention.

    References
    Bhatt–Mathew, The arc-topology

    Serre, Géométrie algébrique et géométrie analytique

    Permalink · Grothendieck diagram

    G000058Rigid analytic admissible G-topologySite

    Analytic geometry · Structure · Rigid analytic spaces in the sense of Tate

    The site uses admissible open subspaces and admissible coverings. On affinoids the admissible cover condition is tested using finite affinoid refinements; arbitrary unions of point sets do not supply the cover condition.

    References
    Conrad, Several approaches to non-archimedean geometry · nLab, G-topology (bibliographic index)

    Permalink · Grothendieck diagram

    G000059Rigid analytic pro-étale siteSite

    Analytic geometry · Structure · Locally Noetherian adic spaces in Scholze’s framework

    The site uses pro-étale objects obtained locally from inverse systems of étale objects with eventual finite étale transition maps, using the coverings of Scholze §3. This is distinct from the weakly étale scheme site.

    References
    Scholze, p-adic Hodge theory for rigid-analytic varieties

    Permalink · Grothendieck diagram

    G000063Adic tame siteSite

    Analytic geometry · Structure · Adic spaces in Hübner’s setting

    A variant of the étale site with the tameness of the induced extensions of residue valuations built into the morphisms. Its role and comparison with étale cohomology are developed in the cited construction.

    References
    Hübner, The adic tame site

    Permalink · Grothendieck diagram

    G000084Huber adic spectrum topologyTopology

    Analytic geometry · Structure · An adic spectrum Spa(A,A⁺) of a Huber pair

    Points are continuous valuations up to equivalence that are at most 1 on A⁺. Rational subsets, specified by finitely many inequalities ∣fi∣≤∣g∣≠0|f_i|\le |g|\ne0 with the open-ideal condition, form a basis of quasi-compact opens. The adic spectrum is spectral.

    References
    Huber, Continuous valuations, §3

    Permalink · Grothendieck diagram

    G000085Berkovich spectrum topologyTopology

    Analytic geometry · Structure · Berkovich spectrum of a non-Archimedean affinoid algebra A

    Points are bounded multiplicative seminorms with the prescribed restriction to the base field. The topology is initial for the evaluations x↦∣f(x)∣x\mapsto |f(x)| with f in A. This ordinary point-set topology is distinct from the rigid admissible site.

    References
    Berkovich, Spectral Theory and Analytic Geometry over Non-Archimedean Fields · Temkin, Introduction to Berkovich analytic spaces

    Permalink · Grothendieck diagram

    G000060Étale site of a locally spatial diamondSite

    Covers are jointly surjective étale families. For an analytic adic space in Scholze’s construction, the associated diamond has the equivalent étale site described in §15.

    G000065Cdarc topologyTopology

    Motivic and valuative descent · Structure · Qcqs schemes in the motivic excision setting

    Completely decomposed analogue of the arc topology. Use the lifting condition against rank at most one valuation rings specified in the cited definition; the complete decomposition condition is essential.

    Permalink · Grothendieck diagram

    G000066Motivic Nisnevich presentationConstruction

    Motivic and valuative descent · Construction · Smooth schemes over a base S

    Start from Nisnevich sheaves of spaces and impose A¹-invariance by localization at the projections X × A¹ → X. This localization is additional to the sheaf condition.

    References
    Voevodsky, Unstable motivic homotopy categories in Nisnevich and cdh-topologies · Morel–Voevodsky, A¹-homotopy theory of schemes

    Permalink · Grothendieck diagram

    G000079Finite presentation h topologyTopology

    Motivic and valuative descent · Structure · Schemes over a base in the Stacks Project convention

    Covering sieves admit, locally on affine opens of the target, refinement by finite affine covers of a proper surjection of finite presentation. This separates the finite presentation h convention from ph, which uses proper surjections without the finite presentation hypothesis.

    References
    Stacks 0ETQ · the h topology · Stacks 0DBC · the ph topology

    Stacks index 0ETQ 0DBC

    G000080Pro-Nisnevich siteSite

    Motivic and valuative descent · Structure · Mattis’s category of pro-smooth schemes over S

    Covering families are pro-étale, fpqc, and completely decomposed on their disjoint union: every target point lifts with unchanged residue field. The paper compares the resulting ∞-topos with the smooth Nisnevich ∞-topos.

    References
    Mattis, The pro-Nisnevich topology, Definition 2.2

    Permalink · Grothendieck diagram

    G000081Pro-cdh site on schemesSite

    Motivic and valuative descent · Structure · Finite presentation schemes over a qcqs base S

    Generate the topology by distinguished Nisnevich covers and pro-abstract blowup covers. For a proper map that is an isomorphism off a finitely presented closed subscheme, the latter family includes the proper map and all infinitesimal thickenings of the center.

    References
    Kelly–Saito, A procdh topology, Definitions 1.1 and 2.1

    Related theorems · 1

    G000082Pro-cdh site on formal schemesSite

    Motivic and valuative descent · Structure · Formal schemes in the finite-type category specified by Kelly and Saito

    Use Nisnevich covers and formal abstract blowup covers. This presentation uses the formal completion at a center in the formal scheme category; the pro-cdh site on ordinary schemes uses the family of its finite thickenings.

    References
    Kelly–Saito, A pro-cdh topology on formal schemes

    Derived and spectral geometry 4

    G000067Derived étale siteSite

    Derived and spectral geometry · Structure · Opposite category of connective derived commutative rings, or relative version

    In the connective setting an étale map has étale π₀ and the higher homotopy groups are obtained by base change along π₀. A covering family is detected by joint surjectivity on the ordinary spectra. Use the chosen derived ring model and sheaves of spaces.

    References
    Toën–Vezzosi, Homotopical Algebraic Geometry II, §2.2 · Lurie, Spectral Algebraic Geometry

    Permalink · Grothendieck diagram

    G000068Spectral étale siteSite

    Derived and spectral geometry · Structure · Opposite category of connective E∞-rings, or relative version

    Étaleness is characterized by étale π₀ and base change for the homotopy groups; covers are detected on ordinary spectra of π₀. Spectral here refers to ring spectra, a different usage from Hochster’s spectral spaces.

    References
    Lurie, Spectral Algebraic Geometry

    Permalink · Grothendieck diagram

    G000069Derived fppf topologyTopology

    Derived and spectral geometry · Structure · Derived affine schemes in the connective convention

    Use flat locally finitely presented morphisms, with flatness detected by π₀ flatness and base change on higher homotopy, and joint surjectivity on ordinary spectra. This uses homotopical descent, not just set-valued gluing.

    References
    Toën–Vezzosi, Homotopical Algebraic Geometry II, §2.2 · Lurie, Spectral Algebraic Geometry

    Permalink · Grothendieck diagram

    G000086Spectral Zariski siteSite

    Derived and spectral geometry · Structure · Opposite of connective E∞-rings, or relative version

    Basic opens of an affine spectral scheme come from inverting elements of π₀. A family of such localizations covers when the corresponding basic opens cover the ordinary spectrum of π₀.

    References
    Lurie, Spectral Algebraic Geometry

    T000031Valuative (v) topology is coarser than Arc topologyImplication

    Valuative topology refinement · The common qcqs ambient category specified in the valuative diagram.

    The valuation test can be expressed as lifting the specialization from the generic point to the closed point after base change to a valuation spectrum. Over a rank-one valuation ring, lifting that pair of points yields an extension of rank one. Thus an arbitrary-rank cover satisfies the rank-at-most-one test. See Proposition 2.1 and Corollary 2.5 of Bhatt–Mathew.

    T000520Exactness of module localizationConstruction

    Modules

    Hypotheses. Let RR be a ring, U⊆RU\subseteq R a multiplicative subset, and L→M→NL\to M\to N an exact sequence of RR-modules.

    The localized sequence U−1L→U−1M→U−1NU^{-1}L\to U^{-1}M\to U^{-1}N is exact.

    Proof and context

    An element sent to zero in a localization is killed by a denominator. Clearing such a denominator reduces exactness in the middle to exactness before localization.

    See also: Localization of a module, Flat module

    T000521Flatness under base changeCriterion

    Modules

    Hypotheses. Let R→R′R\to R' be any ring map and MM an RR-module. Let M′=R′⊗RMM'=R'\otimes_R M.

    If MM is flat over RR, then M′M' is flat over R′R'. If MM is faithfully flat over RR, then M′M' is faithfully flat over R′R'.

    Proof and context

    On R′R'-modules the functor M′⊗R′−M'\otimes_{R'}- identifies with M⊗R−M\otimes_R-. This transfers preservation of exactness and, in the faithful case, reflection of exactness.

    See also: Flat module, Faithfully flat module

    T000522Faithfully flat descent of module flatnessEquivalence

    Modules

    Hypotheses. Let R→R′R\to R' be faithfully flat and MM an RR-module.

    MM is flat over RR if and only if R′⊗RMR'\otimes_R M is flat over R′R'.

    Proof and context

    Apply base change to a sequence obtained by tensoring an injection with MM. Faithfully flat base change detects the vanishing of its kernel.

    See also: Flat module

    T000523Faithfully flat descent of module finiteness and presentationEquivalence

    Modules

    Hypotheses. Let R→R′R\to R' be faithfully flat, and let MM be an RR-module.

    Finite generation of MM over RR is equivalent to finite generation of R′⊗RMR'\otimes_R M over R′R'. The analogous equivalence holds for finite presentation.

    Proof and context

    Choose finitely many elements of MM whose scalar extensions generate. Faithful flatness detects surjectivity. For finite presentation apply the finite-generation argument to the kernel of a finite free surjection.

    See also: Finite module, Finitely presented module

    T000525Support as a vanishing setCriterion

    Modules

    Hypotheses. Let RR be a ring and MM a finite RR-module.

    Supp⁡R(M)=V(Ann⁡R(M))\operatorname{Supp}_R(M)=V(\operatorname{Ann}_R(M)).

    Proof and context

    If a localization of the module vanishes, each generator is killed by some element outside the prime. The product kills the whole module and remains outside the prime.

    See also: Support of a module, Finite module, Module with closed support

    T000526Computing depth using ExtCriterion

    Modules

    Hypotheses. Let (R,𝔪)(R,\mathfrak m) be a Noetherian local ring and MM a nonzero finite RR-module.

    The depth with respect to 𝔪\mathfrak m is the least nonnegative integer ii such that Ext⁡Ri(R/𝔪,M)≠0\operatorname{Ext}^i_R(R/\mathfrak m,M)\ne 0.

    Proof and context

    Start in degree zero with the criterion for an element annihilated by the ideal. The exact sequence for quotienting by a regular element of the ideal reduces the remaining degrees by one.

    See also: Depth with respect to an ideal, Finite module

    T000527Fixed local rank via Fitting idealsCriterion

    Modules

    Hypotheses. Let MM be a finite RR-module and fix a nonnegative integer rr.

    MM is finite locally free of rank rr if and only if Fit⁡r−1(M)=0\operatorname{Fit}_{r-1}(M)=0 and Fit⁡r(M)=R\operatorname{Fit}_r(M)=R.

    Proof and context

    The minors test the presentation on localizations at primes. In a local presentation with a minimal generating family, the two conditions give precisely the stated free rank.

    See also: Fitting ideals of a module, Finite locally free module of a prescribed rank

    T000529Faithfully flat descent of algebra finiteness and presentationEquivalence

    Ring homomorphisms

    Hypotheses. Let R→SR\to S be a ring map and R→R′R\to R' faithfully flat. Put S′=R′⊗RSS'=R'\otimes_R S.

    R→SR\to S has finite type if and only if R′→S′R'\to S' has finite type. The analogous equivalence holds for finite presentation.

    Proof and context

    Descend algebra generators using faithful flatness. For finite presentation, apply descent for finite modules to the defining ideal after choosing a finite polynomial presentation.

    T000535Classification of étale algebras over a fieldEquivalence

    Ring homomorphisms

    Hypotheses. Let kk be a field and SS a kk-algebra.

    k→Sk\to S is étale if and only if SS is a finite product of finite separable field extensions of kk. The empty product gives the zero algebra.

    Proof and context

    An étale algebra has finite-dimensional fibre over the unique point of the field, and its local factors are separable fields. Conversely, the product of finitely many such field extensions is étale.

    See also: Étale ring map, Finite étale ring map

    T000365Independence of distinct multiplicative charactersCriterion

    Fields

    Hypotheses. Let FF be a field and GG a monoid. Let χ1,…,χn:G→(F,⋅)\chi_1,\dots,\chi_n:G\to(F,\cdot) be distinct monoid homomorphisms.

    These functions are linearly independent over FF. In particular, distinct embeddings of an extension into FF are FF-linearly independent as functions when their common domain and base are fixed.

    Proof and context

    In a nontrivial linear relation of minimal support, compare the relation at ghgh with the relation at hh multiplied by one of the character values at gg. Choose gg on which two characters in the support differ. Subtraction gives a nonzero relation with smaller support.

    T000361Decomposition of an inseparable irreducible polynomialCriterion

    Polynomials over fields

    Hypotheses. Let PP be an inseparable irreducible polynomial over a field FF.

    The characteristic is p>0p>0. There is a maximal power q=prq=p^r with P(T)=Q(Tq)P(T)=Q(T^q), and QQ is irreducible and separable. The distinct roots of PP correspond to the distinct roots of QQ by the map x↦xqx\mapsto x^q in an algebraic closure.

    Proof and context

    If the derivative is zero, all exponents with nonzero coefficient are multiples of pp. Remove the largest common pp-power from those exponents. The resulting derivative is nonzero and irreducibility descends to QQ. Frobenius is bijective in the algebraic closure.

    See also: Irreducible polynomial, Separable irreducible polynomial, Separable degree of an irreducible polynomial

    T000577A pth-root test in a separable algebraic extensionCriterion

    Elements of field extensions

    Hypotheses. Let E/FE/F be separable algebraic in characteristic p>0p>0 and let a∈Ea\in E. Assume aa is a root of a polynomial P∈F[T]P\in F[T] with distinct roots in an algebraic closure and coefficients in FpF^p.

    The element aa is a ppth power in EE. This applies in particular if its minimal polynomial over FF has all coefficients in FpF^p.

    Proof and context

    Take ppth roots of the coefficients of PP to obtain a polynomial QQ with distinct roots. A ppth root of aa is a root of QQ. If it were absent from EE, the irreducible polynomial Tp−aT^p-a over EE would divide QQ, contradicting distinct roots.

    See also: Separable algebraic element, Minimal polynomial, Separable algebraic extension

    T000542Vector space dimension of a rational function fieldCriterion

    Field extensions

    Hypotheses. Let TT be transcendental over the field FF.

    The extension F(T)/FF(T)/F is infinite-dimensional. For an infinite field FF it has dimension ∣F∣|F|.

    Proof and context

    The monomials give an infinite independent family. For each a∈Fa\in F, the functions 1/(T−a)1/(T-a) are linearly independent: clear the denominators in a finite relation and evaluate in turn at the corresponding values aa. The number of rational functions is at most ∣F∣|F| when FF is infinite.

    See also: Rational function field, Degree of an extension, Finite field extension

    T000544Function field of a compact Riemann surfaceCriterion

    Field extensions

    Hypotheses. Let XX be a compact connected Riemann surface and ff a nonconstant meromorphic function on XX.

    The field 𝐂(X)\mathbf C(X) is algebraic over 𝐂(f)\mathbf C(f). It has transcendence degree one over 𝐂\mathbf C.

    Proof and context

    A nonconstant meromorphic function defines a finite holomorphic map to the sphere. For a meromorphic function on the source, the elementary symmetric functions in its values on the sheets define meromorphic coefficients on the sphere, giving an algebraic equation.

    T000364Counting embeddings along a generating towerCriterion

    Field extensions

    Hypotheses. Let E=F(a1,…,an)E=F(a_1,\dots,a_n) with each aia_i algebraic over FF, and set Fi=F(a1,…,ai)F_i=F(a_1,\dots,a_i). Let PiP_i be the minimal polynomial of aia_i over Fi−1F_{i-1}. Fix an algebraic closure F‾\overline F.

    At each step, after choosing an embedding of Fi−1F_{i-1}, the image of aia_i can be any distinct root of the transported PiP_i. This gives ∏i=1ndeg⁡s(Pi)\prod_{i=1}^n\deg_s(P_i) embeddings of EE over FF. Their number equals [E:F][E:F] if every step is separable and is smaller if some step is inseparable.

    Proof and context

    The universal property of the simple-extension presentation gives one lift per root. The number of roots of the transported polynomial is the separable degree. Compare the product with the tower law.

    See also: Finite field extension, Separable degree of an extension, Separable degree of an irreducible polynomial

    T000371A finite purely inseparable extension is built from pth rootsCriterion

    Field extensions

    Hypotheses. Let E/FE/F be finite purely inseparable with characteristic p>0p>0.

    There is a finite tower from FF to EE whose nontrivial steps have degree pp and are obtained by adjoining a ppth root. Consequently [E:F][E:F] is a power of pp.

    Proof and context

    If an element is outside the current field, take its penultimate pp-power for a minimal exponent that puts a power into that field. This produces a degree-pp step by the missing-root criterion. Finite degree bounds the number of steps.

    Sites and presentations 64

    T000097The finite qc basis presents Zariski sheavesComparison

    Sites and presentations

    Every open is a union of affine opens. Finite intersections of quasi-compact opens are quasi-compact on a quasi-separated scheme, and every open covering of a basis object has a finite basis refinement. Restriction and the usual compatible-section extension therefore give inverse equivalences of sheaf categories.

    See also: Qcqs scheme, Qc Zariski basis site

    T000098Two uses of qc in site terminologyComparison

    Sites and presentations

    The finite open basis site uses inclusions of open subsets of a fixed scheme. The Stacks qc topology in Cohomology on Sites §21.31 uses continuous maps between locally quasi-compact Hausdorff spaces. Its comparison theorem uses the latter hypotheses, so it does not automatically apply to the Zariski space of a qcqs scheme.

    See also: Qc Zariski basis site, Qc topology on locally quasi-compact spaces

    T000100The profinite site and condensed setsComparison

    Sites and presentations

    Finite jointly surjective families are closed under pullback and composition, and include the empty family covering the empty space. With a fixed strong limit size bound, the sheaf condition on this site gives the corresponding condensed sets. This compares sites of spaces and is not a refinement relation on schemes.

    T000101Comparison with a basisComparison

    Sites and presentations

    For a qcqs scheme the quasi-compact opens form a basis closed under finite intersections. The basis comparison lemma identifies sheaves on all opens with sheaves for the induced basis topology; each cover of a quasi-compact open admits a finite subcover.

    See also: Grothendieck site, Petit Zariski site, Qc Zariski basis site

    T000102Giraud’s characterizationComparison

    Sites and presentations

    A Grothendieck topos is characterized, in a fixed universe, by the Giraud axioms: a small generating family, universal small colimits, disjoint coproducts and effective equivalence relations (with the usual categorical hypotheses). A site gives a presentation, not a unique presentation.

    See also: Grothendieck topos, Grothendieck site

    References

    Pullback along a universal homeomorphism of schemes is an equivalence of small étale sites and yields an equivalence of étale topoi. This statement does not identify the structure sheaves as rings under arbitrary such maps.

    T000104Hochster representationEquivalence

    Sites and presentations

    Hypotheses. Work in classical set theory. Consider a topological space XX and commutative rings with identity, allowing the zero ring.

    XX is spectral if and only if it is homeomorphic to Spec⁡(A)\operatorname{Spec}(A) for some commutative ring AA. The equivalence concerns existence of a realization as a topological space.

    Proof and context

    Every spectral space is homeomorphic to the prime spectrum of a commutative ring, and every prime spectrum is spectral. The assertion concerns the underlying topological space, without specifying a canonical ring or recovering a scheme structure.

    See also: Spectral space, Affine, Coherent locale, Prime spectrum of a ring

    References
    Hochster, Prime ideal structure in commutative rings (1969) · Stacks 08YF · spectral spaces and the constructible topology · Hochster, Prime ideal structure in commutative rings, Theorem 6 · Stacks 08YG · definition of spectral space

    T000105Coherent locale and spectral space dualityEquivalence

    Sites and presentations

    Hypotheses. Use classical prime ideal separation, spectral spaces with spectral maps, and coherent locales with maps whose inverse image preserves compact opens.

    Taking the locale of opens and taking the space of points are inverse equivalences. The compact elements of the frame are the quasi-compact opens of the spectral space.

    Proof and context

    Classically, bounded distributive lattices are dual to spectral spaces with spectral maps. Prime ideals give the points, and the lattice is recovered as the quasi-compact opens. Ideal completion gives the corresponding coherent frame; the spatial interpretation uses classical prime ideal separation.

    See also: Locale, Coherent locale, Spectral map, Spectral space

    References

    In the dual topology the quasi-compact opens are the complements of the original quasi-compact opens. Taking complements twice proves involutivity and adjoining both families gives the same patch topology.

    T000109Little and big Zariski comparisonSite comparison

    Sites and presentations

    Hypotheses. Let SS be a scheme. Choose a big Zariski site as in Blechschmidt §15, containing the opens of SS, and let Sh⁡(S)\operatorname{Sh}(S) denote the little Zariski topos.

    The geometric morphism π:Zar⁡(S)→Sh⁡(S)\pi:\operatorname{Zar}(S)\to\operatorname{Sh}(S) is connected and local. The direct image π∗\pi_* is restriction and has a fully faithful right adjoint, giving a section of π\pi.

    Proof and context

    For the big site chosen in the thesis, §16 constructs the comparison with the little topos and describes how the structure sheaves and internal statements transform. The restricted affine finite presentation model has its own specified hypotheses and is not being identified here with the entire category of schemes over an arbitrary base.

    Sites and presentations

    Hypotheses. Let 𝒞\mathcal C be a site specified by covering families satisfying the isomorphism, composition and base-change axioms.

    The axioms on the families give the maximal-sieve, pullback and local-character axioms. A matching family on a cover extends to its generated sieve by compatibility on the pullbacks.     Sites and presentations

    Hypotheses. Let JJ and J′J' be Grothendieck topologies on the same category 𝒞\mathcal C, with the same ambient presheaf category.

    Hypotheses. Let the presheaves and sheaves be set-valued on a site.

    The sheafification functor preserves finite limits and all small colimits.

    The plus construction uses directed colimits over refinements. Finite limits in sets commute with these colimits and with the limits imposing compatibility on matching families. Applying plus twice gives preservation of finite limits. The adjunction gives preservation of colimits.

    T000152Comparison lemma for sitesEquivalence

    Sites and presentations

    Hypotheses. Let u:𝒞→𝒟u:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D be continuous and cocontinuous. Require that two arrows with the same image under uu agree after a cover of their common source, and that an arrow u(U′)→u(U)u(U')\to u(U) locally lifts after a cover of U′U' in 𝒞\mathcal C. Require every object of 𝒟\mathcal D to have a cover by objects in the image of uu.

    The morphism Sh⁡(𝒞)→Sh⁡(𝒟)\operatorname{Sh}(\mathcal C)\to\operatorname{Sh}(\mathcal D) obtained from the cocontinuous functor uu is an equivalence.

    Proof and context

    Local lifting and equality of arrows identify the sheafified morphism data on image objects. The covering condition then reconstructs each sheaf on the target from those local data by descent.

    T000153Subcanonical presentation by sheafified representablesEquivalence

    Sites and presentations

    Hypotheses. Let 𝒞′\mathcal C' be a small full subcategory of Sh⁡(𝒞)\operatorname{Sh}(\mathcal C) containing the sheafified representables hU#h_U^\# and closed under fibre products in the sheaf category.

    The families in 𝒞′\mathcal C' with epimorphic coproduct map form a subcanonical site presentation. The functor U↦hU#U\mapsto h_U^\# induces Sh⁡(𝒞)≃Sh⁡(𝒞′)\operatorname{Sh}(\mathcal C)\simeq\operatorname{Sh}(\mathcal C').

    Proof and context

    Epimorphisms of sheaves are effective and stable under pullback, so representables satisfy descent for the specified families. The original covers induce such epimorphisms, and the hU#h_U^\# generate the sheaf category. The resulting functor satisfies the site comparison hypotheses.

    T000155Geometric stalks on small and big étale sitesConstruction

    Sites and presentations

    Hypotheses. Let SS be a scheme, with the big site formed in a fixed size convention.

    The geometric points of SS give a conservative family for the small étale site. On the big étale site use the geometric points of all objects T→ST\to S, evaluating the stalk after restriction to TeˊtT_{\text{ét}}. Exactness of sequences of abelian sheaves on the small site is equivalent to exactness at the geometric stalks.

    Proof and context

    A stalk is the filtered colimit over pointed étale neighbourhoods. A germ that lifts or vanishes does so after shrinking such a neighbourhood. Doing this above every point gives the covering family that witnesses the local sheaf condition for surjectivity or injectivity. On the big site these tests are made object by object.

    T000163Finite sober inverse limits characterize spectral spacesEquivalence

    Sites and presentations

    Hypotheses. Let the limit be taken in topological spaces over a directed inverse system.

    A space is spectral if and only if it can be presented as an inverse limit of finite sober spaces.

    Proof and context

    A spectral space embeds in a product of Sierpiński spaces using its quasi-compact opens, with patch-closed image. Its projections to finite coordinate sets give finite sober spaces. Patch compactness identifies the image with the compatible tuples in these projections, and the finite-coordinate opens recover the spectral topology. Conversely, directed limits of finite sober spaces are spectral.

    See also: Spectral space, Sober space, Spectral map, Constructible topology

    T000353Algebraicity in towersCriterion

    Hypotheses. Let F⊆E⊆LF\subseteq E\subseteq L be field extensions and let a∈La\in L.

    Examples and counterexamples

    Commutative rings 12

    X000024The zero ringExample

    Commutative rings

    It has a single ideal, no prime ideals, and no nonzero nilpotent elements. Its prime-localization conditions are vacuous. It has no proper maximal ideal.

    X000054An extension that cannot be generated by countably many elementsExample

    Field extensions

    The field generated over 𝐐\mathbf Q by a countable set is countable, since every element is represented by a rational expression in finitely many generators. The complex numbers are uncountable. An algebraic extension of 𝐐\mathbf Q is countable by the cardinality bound.

    Has: Base field of characteristic zero, Algebraically closed target field
    Fails: Countably generated field extension, Finitely generated field extension, Algebraic field extension, Finite field extension

    Ring–ideal pairs 1

    X000055The localized integers: idempotents lift but the pair is not henselianExample

    Ring–ideal pairs

    Take (A,I)=(𝐙(2),2𝐙(2))(A,I)=(\mathbf Z_{(2)},2\mathbf Z_{(2)}). The ideal is maximal and both the local ring and its residue field have only the idempotents zero and one. But T2−T+2T^2-T+2 reduces to the product T(T−1)T(T-1) of comaximal monic factors, while it has no rational root, since its discriminant is −7-7. A lifted monic factorization would consist of linear factors.

    Has: Ideal in the Jacobson radical, Idempotent bijection for the pair
    Fails: Lifting comaximal monic factorizations, Henselian pair

    X000011A two-point spectral space that is not profiniteExample

    Topological spaces

    The spectrum of a discrete valuation ring has one generic point and one closed point. It is spectral, but the generic point is not closed. In the patch topology both singletons are open, so that topology is finite discrete.

    Has: Spectral space
    Fails: T₁ space, Hausdorff space, Profinite space

    X000012A compact Hausdorff space that is not profiniteExample

    Topological spaces

    The real interval [0,1] is compact and Hausdorff, but connected and has more than one point. It cannot be profinite, since the finite discrete coordinate quotients of a profinite space separate its points.

    Has: Quasi-compact space, Hausdorff space
    Fails: Totally disconnected space, Profinite space, Spectral space

    Stacks 08ZY · profinite spaces

    X000014The p-adic integers are profinite but not extremally disconnectedExample

    Topological spaces

    The p-adic integers are the inverse limit of the finite discrete quotient rings modulo powers of p. The subset of nonzero elements with even p-adic valuation is open. Its closure adds 0, which is not interior because every neighbourhood of 0 also contains elements of odd valuation.

    Has: Profinite space
    Fails: Extremally disconnected space

    Sources and method

    The catalogue records hypotheses and primary references. Browse all 21,446 registered tags in the Stacks Project index, with bidirectional source references and definition clauses. Source references are editorially distinct from implications.

    Codes are local to this atlas and independent of display order. P identifies a predicate; G a structure or construction; T a theorem; X an example. Pi-Base links show their own external IDs and indicate whether the definition is the same, applies to the underlying space, or only gives a comparison. Search Pi-Base P000050 to match that external ID specifically.

    Within each refinement diagram, “A is coarser than B” means every A-covering sieve is B-covering in the stated category. The checker compiles conjunctions to Horn clauses, indexes occurrences by signed fact, and records a proof step for each inference. It can use an explicit negative hypothesis or test the opposite of the goal by refutation. Incompatible premises are reported as such. A counterexample requires a cited object satisfying all hypotheses and failing the conclusion. An unresolved result is unknown in the recorded theory.

    Comparisons across categories and results whose hypotheses have no machine-readable encoding are presented as references. The inference is relative to the verified rules in the catalogue; it is not a decision procedure for algebraic geometry.

    Predicate entries separate the object domain, hypotheses and conclusion. One Stacks definition can give rise to several distinct predicates. Conjunctions and stated equivalences join predicates without merging their IDs. The explicit logical presentation takes inspiration from Blechschmidt’s account of internal languages; the implication checker is classical and uses only the explicitly stated scope.

    Design references: Grassmannian.info’s classification and item-level bibliography · Pi-Base record format · Pi-Base prover · Dowling–Gallier, Horn clauses.

    Cohomology reading guides: Holmström’s crystalline index and étale index; see also Berthelot, Cohomologie cristalline and Milne, Lectures on Étale Cohomology.
